analysis.one_liner: Creates ethics advisors and investigators with subpoena power inside the Supreme Court.
analysis.headline: Ten House Democrats introduced the bill on February 25, 2026; it has sat in the Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create two new offices inside the Supreme Court: one to advise the justices on ethics questions like gifts, financial disclosure, and conflicts of interest, and one to investigate ethics complaints against justices, with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents. Findings would go to the Chief Justice and to congressional committees, and evidence of crimes would be referred to the Attorney General. The bill has only been introduced and sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who expect the nine Supreme Court justices to follow the same ethics rules they expect of other officials. The bill would give justices professional ethics advice on gifts, financial disclosures, political activity, and recusal [S2], and create an office with subpoena power that investigates ethics complaints and reports findings to Congress [S2]. The public would see annual statistics on how often justices seek ethics advice and whether they follow it [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public seeking Supreme Court accountability

how_it_helps.text: Each justice would take ethics training twice a year covering gifts, financial disclosure, conflicts, recusal, and political activity

A standing Office of Investigative Counsel would review ethics complaints against justices or their spouses and dependents, open full investigations within 15 days of a determination, and use subpoena power backed by contempt of court to compel testimony and documents
Investigative findings and recommendations — including recusal or divestment — would be shared with the House and Senate Judiciary Committees and relevant oversight committees within 10 days
If the office finds reasonable grounds to believe a justice broke federal criminal law, it must report expeditiously to the Attorney General
The public would get an annual accounting of how often justices sought ethics advice, on what topics, and how often the advice was not followed

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new offices — the bill sets minimum salaries of $225,000 for the top counsels and $180,000 for other counsels [S2]. The justices themselves would bear the cost of oversight: gift-taking, financial disclosures, and conflicts of interest would for the first time be reviewed by dedicated staff with the power to investigate and subpoena records [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers funding the new ethics offices

drawbacks.text: The Chief Justice — the official whose conduct could be investigated — appoints every counsel, pays them, can fire them only for cause, and in his sole discretion decides whether investigative reports become public; complaints can only be filed by congressional leaders, not ordinary citizens

Critics argue Congress cannot lawfully restructure the Court's internal operations this way, since the Constitution gives the judiciary independence from congressional control of its core functions; the bill includes a severability clause anticipating court challenges

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost is small — a handful of salaried attorneys within the Court's existing budget. The accountability gain is real but limited by design: the person with the most power over the new offices is the Chief Justice, the same official whose conduct they would investigate, and reports reach the public only if he chooses to release them. The bill would create meaningful paper trails and congressional visibility that do not exist today, but it stops short of independent enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2026 by Rep. Daniel Goldman with nine Democratic cosponsors
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action has been taken since the referral

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost: the bill has simply gone nowhere. The Supreme Court continues under its existing arrangement, in which the justices police their own conduct with no independent investigative body.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 25, 2026 and has taken no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no Republican has signed on, making this an entirely one-party initiative so far.

industries.note: The bill would place the justices' gifts, travel, financial disclosures, and recusal decisions under scrutiny by professional staff for the first time, with the power to investigate and subpoena. Justices currently rely on self-enforcement of the Court's own code of conduct.

The bill would create roughly a dozen permanent, well-paid government positions ($225,000 for chiefs, $180,000 minimum for others) filled by outside attorneys, a modest new revenue channel for the legal profession.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. It has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing, no markup, and no Republican cosponsors; bills at this stage with one-party support routinely expire when the Congress ends without ever reaching the floor.
